title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Mill in Motion: Introduction to Dorlcote

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over this series we're taking George Eliot's great novel apart — passage by passage, image by image — to understand how it works and why it endures.
Today we begin at the beginning: the world of Dorlcote Mill, the Tulliver family, and the extraordinary child at the centre of it all.
Three guests join me, and I want to introduce them properly, because each brings something quite distinct to the table.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a literary critic and novelist who teaches creative writing — she reads with a craftsman's eye, always asking how the effect is achieved, never content just to enjoy it.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don of the old school — steeped in moral philosophy, devoted to questions of character and goodness, and beautifully sceptical of fashionable readings.

And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels for audio than almost anyone alive — he hears fiction the way a conductor hears a score, and his feel for Eliot's comic timing is frankly unmatched.
Let's go straight to Maggie Tulliver — aged eight, already impossible to contain.
What strikes me immediately about these early Maggie passages is how Eliot refuses to sentimentalise the child even as she clearly adores her.
There's this extraordinary double movement in the narration — warmth and irony running in perfect parallel.
Look at how she sets up Maggie's grand resolution to flee to the gypsies.
"Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined."
"As usual" — two words that do the work of a whole character study.
Eliot is both laughing at Maggie and honouring her — that tension is the engine of everything that follows.
Eleanor's absolutely right, and as someone who has spoken these words aloud in a recording booth, I can tell you that "as usual" is a gift to the narrator.
There's a tiny comic beat built right into the syntax — you can feel the narrator suppressing a smile.
And then Eliot gives you the full flight of Maggie's fantasy — the gypsies who will receive her with respect on account of her superior knowledge.
The phrase "superior knowledge" is doing something marvellous — it's both Maggie's own self-description and Eliot's gentle mockery of it.
But then — and this is where I always feel for her — she arrives among the gypsies and the dream detonates.
The narrator tells us, with perfectly straight-faced horror, that Maggie had begun to think the gypsies meant — and I have to read this —
"to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking." I defy you to find a funnier, more terrifying two-word phrase in Victorian fiction.
Oliver's delight is infectious and entirely warranted.
But I want to hold onto something rather serious beneath the comedy — which is that Maggie's escapism is already a symptom of her deepest problem.
She cannot endure reproach — she must flee from it rather than face it and discipline her will.
Eliot is quite precise about this — and the passage on Maggie's education makes it plain.
"Her thoughts generally were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams."
That, I think, is the novel's central diagnosis — announced early and confirmed throughout.
The tragedy is not society's failure to accommodate Maggie — it is Maggie's failure to accommodate reality.
Edmund, I'd push back on that just slightly — not on the diagnosis, which is exact, but on where the weight of the novel's sympathy falls.
Because look at what Eliot does with the etymology passage — the detail about Maggie deducing that "poly" must mean "many" because she knows both "polygamy" and "polysyllable."
That is a child thinking — genuinely thinking, rigorously — with the materials she has been given.
The narrator describes it as unexpected ignorance alongside unexpected knowledge — and both words are doing equal work.
The irony cuts at the world that has left her with so few books she reads the dictionary — not only at Maggie herself.
And Tom feels it, too — that's the quietly devastating thing.
When Maggie is finally fetched away from his school in the gig, Eliot records the effect on Tom with real tenderness.
"He had really been brighter, and had got through his lessons better, since she had been there."
He missed her grievously — and that word "grievously" is not comic at all.
Eliot is already preparing us for the weight of what the relationship between these two children will eventually carry.
And that, precisely, is where Eliot's moral imagination is at its finest.
Tom is not merely the dull, constraining brother — he is genuinely enlarged by Maggie's presence, even if he cannot say so.
Eliot shows us that Maggie's questions about the Roman Empire had given Tom a luminous idea — her phrase — that his textbooks never could.
"There had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
It is a gentle comedy, yes — but also a genuine expansion of a boy's mind, administered by a girl the world considers ungovernable.
That image of Maggie as this ungovernable, impractical, voraciously intelligent child — it's the foundation everything else is built on.
In the next segment, we'll look at the Tulliver household itself — the mill, the river, the family, and the social world pressing in from outside.

segments.title: The Architecture of Minds: Maggie and Tom's Intellectual Divide

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the series that takes George Eliot's great novel apart sentence by sentence to ask how it works and why it endures.
Today we're deep inside the novel's most painful territory: the intellectual and moral divide between Maggie and Tom Tulliver.
How does Eliot build two minds so differently, and what does the collision between them cost?
With me today are three readers who bring very different tools to these questions.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and teacher of creative writing who sees the architecture behind every fictional effect.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as explorations of individual character tested by circumstance and by conscience.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — comes to every novel first as a performer who hears the prose before he analyses it.
Let's begin at the beginning of this rift — in childhood, where Eliot quietly lays every charge of explosive that will detonate later.
What I love about that early scene with Maggie and little Lucy is the sheer wickedness of Eliot's observation.
She gives us a child in the grip of jealousy and then — with perfectly deadpan precision — she tells us what that jealousy is actually capable of producing.
The narrator sets it up with such apparent tenderness before the knife goes in.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse! A creature so small, so defenceless, so obviously safe from harm — and Eliot puts it there precisely to show us how far Maggie has already travelled from that safety.
Because within two sentences Maggie is fantasising about slapping and pinching Lucy — not out of cruelty, but out of love for Tom, twisted by his indifference.
That is devastating child psychology delivered in three sentences of comic prose.
And notice what Eliot is doing structurally here — the jealousy doesn't attach to Tom directly, because Tom is, as the text admits, of no use to slap.
So it displaces onto Lucy, the nearest available body, the softest available target.
Eliot is mapping the mechanics of resentment with almost clinical accuracy — and doing it through a nine-year-old girl.
What this establishes, very early, is that Maggie's emotional life is constitutively relational.
She cannot feel anything in isolation — every emotion is tangled with someone else, refracted through someone else's response to her.
Tom, by contrast, is being constructed throughout this novel as a mind that seals itself off — that processes the world through rules and categories rather than through feeling.
And the schoolroom chapters show us exactly how that happens.
I want to resist slightly the idea that Tom is simply sealed off or emotionally deficient.
The schoolroom passage is in fact one of the most tender things in the novel, and it is tender precisely about Tom.
Eliot tells us that under Mr. Stelling's rigorous and frankly unsuitable instruction, Tom became — and this is extraordinary — more like a girl than he had ever been in his life.
His pride — which had previously rested quite comfortably on unquestioned local authority — suddenly found nothing but, as Eliot says, bruises and crushings.
And what does this boy do with his humiliation?
He prays. Privately, haltingly, improvising a petition for which he knows of no precedent.
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
There is more genuine pathos in that one whispered clause than in pages of explicit suffering.
Tom is not unfeeling. He is simply in a world — a world of classical education, of masculine expectation — for which his particular intelligence is entirely unsuited.
Edmund is absolutely right about that prayer — when I recorded the novel, that was the moment I had to stop and collect myself.

And then Eliot immediately gives him the follow-up petition about Euclid — asking Mr. Stelling to say he sha'n't do it any more — which is perfectly comic and perfectly heartbreaking in the same breath.
That is the double register she works in constantly: the child's bathos and the adult's tragedy are the same event.
But — and here I do want to push back on Edmund slightly — what happens to this sensitive, bruised Tom is that the bruising sets him.
It hardens into the thing Eliot diagnoses later with devastating clinical precision: the mind that cannot sustain doubt, and so lives on prejudice instead.
That diagnosis is one of the great passages of psychological analysis in Victorian fiction, and I think it deserves to be read aloud in full.
Eliot is describing Tom's mind directly — unflinchingly, without apology.

"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye — however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right."
The phrase that stops me cold every time is that last one: 'the authority of conscious right.'
Tom is never uncertain. He never doubts that he is in the right, and that certainty — which looks like strength — is actually the most terrible thing about him.
And notice that Eliot calls him 'our good, upright Tom Tulliver' — the irony is absolutely controlled, never sneering.
She understands how he got here. She just will not let us excuse what he does with it.
I'll grant the force of that passage. But I would gently observe that Eliot's narrator is not omniscient here in any neutral sense — she is an advocate.
Tom's case is being prosecuted, and Maggie's is being defended, by the same authorial voice.

Consider the confrontation over Philip Wakem, in which Tom accuses Philip with a passion that is — whatever one thinks of its justice — the passion of a man who believes himself entirely in the right of things.
He speaks of Philip's attempt to court Maggie in terms that are extreme, yes — but they come from a coherent, if narrow, moral universe.
He says — and one can hear the genuine indignation —

"you — you to try and worm yourself into the affections of a handsome girl who is not eighteen, and has been shut out from the world by her father's misfortunes! That's your crooked notion of honour, is it?"
Whatever we think of Tom's severity, the material facts he cites are not wrong.
Maggie is isolated, she is young, and the Wakem connexion is genuinely dangerous for the family. Tom's analysis is impoverished — but it is not baseless.
The material facts are not wrong, Edmund, but the mode of enforcement is everything.
Look at what Tom actually requires of Maggie in that confrontation — it's not a conversation, it is an oath.
He demands she place her hand on the Bible and speak the exact words he prescribes, because, as he says —

"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies — working for the respectability of our family — you have done all you can to destroy both."
'No consistency.' That is the charge — and it's the most revealing thing Tom could possibly say.
Because what he means by consistency is conformity to his categories — the categories Eliot has just shown us are built on inherited prejudice and unfed intellect.
Maggie's 'inconsistency' is actually her capacity for growth, for doubt, for revision — the very qualities that make her the novel's heroine and Tom its unwitting villain.
And yet — Maggie's capacity for revision, her openness to new ideas, is also what makes her perpetually vulnerable.

Think about the Thomas à Kempis scene — that extraordinary moment when she picks up the little old clumsy book from a dusty shelf and finds that a hand, now forever quiet, has already marked the passages she needs to hear.
It is the most seductive intellectual moment in the novel — a voice from the past reaching directly into her hunger.
And what does it tell her?
It tells her to renounce. To lay the axe to the root of the love of self.

"Know that the love of thyself doth hurt thee more than anything in the world.... If thou seekest this or that, and wouldst be here or there to enjoy thy own will and pleasure, thou shalt never be quiet nor free from care."
It is balm to a mind that has been told, in effect, that all her wanting is the problem.
Tom tells her she has no consistency. À Kempis tells her to stop wanting altogether. The world offers Maggie no middle ground whatsoever.

That is finely observed — and I think it points to something Eliot understands with great sorrow: that the renunciation doctrine is both genuinely consoling and genuinely insufficient for a mind like Maggie's.
She needs it — it gives her peace, temporarily — but it cannot finally contain her, because her nature is expansive where the doctrine is contractive.
And Tom cannot offer her the alternative. His is the world of fixed boundaries, satisfied duties, debts repaid.
There is a kind of heroism in that — and Eliot does not entirely deny it — but it is heroism of a sort that simply cannot house Maggie's nature.
The tragedy, finally, is not that Tom is evil. The tragedy is that he is exactly what he was made to be — and Maggie is exactly what the world has no category for.
That image of Maggie as someone the world has no category for might be the best summary of this novel I've heard.

We've traced this divide from Maggie's jealousy in childhood, through Tom's humiliation in the schoolroom, to Eliot's devastating anatomy of the rigid mind — and the renunciation that never quite solves what it promises to.

In our next segment, we'll turn to what the river and the flood mean for all of this — whether Eliot's great ending is resolution, or simply the world reasserting that there is no place for someone like Maggie.

segments.title: The Father's Fall: Tulliver's Ruin and Social Consequence

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the currents of pride, money, and family loyalty that run through George Eliot's novel.
And now we arrive at one of the novel's great catastrophes — the ruin of Mr Tulliver.
It is a fall that is at once comic and devastating, shaped by pride, by law, and by the peculiar dynamics of the Tulliver marriage.
With me to unpack it are Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan.
Eleanor — let's begin with the letter Tulliver sends to Mrs Glegg, because it is a masterpiece of catastrophically misplaced pride.
It really is — and what I love is that Eliot sets it up with perfect satirical geometry.
Mrs Glegg has just been luxuriating in her own magnanimity — she's composing herself into a figure of noble forgiveness.
And then Eliot drops the letter in.
The narrator's voice is extraordinary here — that little aside, 'I leave you to judge what effect was produced on her.'
'I leave you to judge what effect was produced on her.'
That is a narrator winking at us over the character's head — pure Eliot.
And then the letter's contents — Tulliver repaying the money, yes, but wrapping it in a declaration of independence that can only wound.
He tells her she is welcome to his house, but he desires no favours — which is the politest possible way of delivering a slap.
'She was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.'
Every word is technically civil and yet constitutes an act of war.
And you can hear it, can't you — when you read it aloud.
There's this tremendous rhythm to Tulliver's indignation — it's always galloping just ahead of his better judgment.
He's repaying the money, which is honourable — and destroying himself in the same breath, which is Tulliver entirely.
I've always thought he's a man who could only exist in a novel — because in real life, someone would have sat on him before now.
With respect to Oliver, I think that's rather the point.
Tulliver is a man of genuine pride — not vanity, which is a lesser thing, but pride rooted in a real sense of his own standing as a man and a father.
The tragedy is that this virtue — and it is a virtue — becomes the instrument of his undoing.
Eliot is profoundly interested in the way a man's strengths and his failures are the same thing, merely observed from different angles.
Edmund, that idea of pride as a double-edged thing connects beautifully to the narrator's extraordinary dissection of Mrs Tulliver's role in all of this.
Because Eliot performs this wonderful sleight of hand — appearing to exonerate Mrs Tulliver and condemning her in the same sentence.
The camel's back passage is one of my favourite pieces of Eliot's narrative mischief.
She sets up the feather metaphor in a way that seems sympathetic to Mrs Tulliver — and then immediately subverts it.
The narrator says her pleading might be comparable to — and here it is:
'that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back.'
Credit or discredit — that's doing enormous work.
Eliot refuses to assign the feather a moral charge — she holds both possibilities open at once.
But then the parenthetical on 'strictly impartial view' lets the narrator slide in and say — actually, the blame lies with all the previous feathers.
Which is a way of distributing culpability so finely that it becomes almost invisible.
And yet — and this is the bit that delights me — there's a steel underneath the comedy.
Because the passage ends with that precise, almost clinical observation about Mr Tulliver's psychology.
Whenever Mrs Tulliver disagreed with him, he saw not his wife — he saw the Dodsons.
And, as Eliot puts it, 'a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.'
That 'even though one of them was Mrs Glegg' — delivered with a perfectly straight face — is one of the great comic asides in English fiction.
It is very fine.
Though I'd observe that the comedy is inseparable from the pathos — because we know where this arithmetic of pride is heading.
What Eliot is mapping, with extraordinary precision, is how a man constructs a world in which his worst decisions feel inevitable — feel, indeed, like acts of honour.
And the law is the great temptation — the arena where Tulliver believes his personal sense of justice can be vindicated by an external authority.
Which brings us to Wakem — the man Tulliver casts as the villain of his personal universe.
Oliver, this is territory you've inhabited professionally — you've read Tulliver's rants from the inside.
Tulliver on Wakem is one of those passages I could read every day and still find something new in it.

Eliot gives you this magnificent parenthetical — 'metaphorically speaking' — dropped into an account of Tulliver's thinking as though his conspiracy theory needs that single caveat to be entirely reasonable.
And then the portrait of Wakem himself — I cannot resist it:
'A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber — always looking so sure of his game!'
That is Tulliver's voice breaking through the narrator's — free indirect discourse at its most vivid.
You can hear his fury — and his slightly helpless awe at Wakem's competence.
The free indirect style in that whole passage is extraordinary — Eliot moves in and out of Tulliver's consciousness without ever losing her own ironic distance.
Notice the phrase — 'Wakem's rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver's interests and opinions.'
That subordinate clause — 'embodied in Mr Tulliver's interests and opinions' — is the whole joke and the whole tragedy.
Tulliver can only conceive of right as what aligns with himself — and Eliot shows us this without ever once nudging us.
The structure of the sentence does the moral work.
And yet — I want to resist the reading that Tulliver is simply foolish.
He is right that Wakem is his adversary — wrong only in the metaphysical scope he assigns to that adversity.
The real question is whether the law — any law — could ever satisfy a man whose quarrel is not with a statute but with the shape of his world.
That shapes exactly the question I want to put to Edmund — because the fall, when it comes, is not only Tulliver's.
The children are pulled into it — and Tom's response in particular is one of the novel's most striking moments of moral seriousness.
Tom Tulliver is, I think, one of the most underestimated characters in the novel.
Readers tend to find him cold — unbending — and he is both of those things.
But in this scene, facing his aunts directly and speaking with a simplicity that shames their fussing about propriety — he is genuinely heroic.
He says to them — and he looks straight at Mrs Glegg as he does so:
'Wouldn't it be better to give it now, and pay the debt we're going to be sold up for, and save my mother from parting with her furniture?'
There is no rhetoric there — no flattery, no appeal to sentiment.
Just a boy — still almost a boy — asking his family to be equal to the name they're so proud of.
The furniture.
Eliot knows that 'furniture' is the most heartbreaking word in that sentence.
It grounds everything in the physical and the domestic — in what Mrs Tulliver has spent her life accumulating and polishing.
Tom could have said 'save my mother from disgrace' — which is what the aunts would understand.
He says 'furniture' — which is what his mother would understand.
And it also tells us something about Tom himself — that he loves his mother in her terms, not in some elevated version of her.
Which makes his later hardness toward Maggie all the more complicated — because he is capable of this quality of attention.
He can see what people actually need — and yet he can also be utterly blind to it.
And that blindness — Edmund, you've been wanting to come to Tom's confrontation with Philip Wakem, I think.
Because it's a scene where the ruin's legacy turns into something much darker.
It is the scene where Tom's virtues curdle — where his sense of family honour becomes something it is harder to admire.
He confronts Philip with an absolute certainty — and that certainty is not entirely wrong, which is what makes it so troubling.
He says — and the prose here is almost polemical in its drive:
'I'll save her from throwing herself away on you — from making herself a laughing-stock — from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son.'
And then — this is the blade:
'You know well enough what sort of justice and cherishing you were preparing for her.'
'Cherishing' — used as an accusation.
Tom takes Philip's own language of devotion and turns it against him — with a brutality that is perfectly lucid.
The thing is — Tom is not entirely wrong.
Wakem senior would not have welcomed Maggie Tulliver as a daughter-in-law — the social arithmetic was as brutal as Tom says.
And yet the delivery — 'I'm not to be imposed upon by fine words; I can see what actions mean' — has all the self-righteousness of a man who has never doubted himself.
He's his father's son — right about the facts, disastrous about the implications.
What arrests me structurally is that Eliot doesn't give us Maggie's response in that moment.
Tom ends with 'Come away, Maggie' — an order, not a question — and the scene closes on him.
It's a brilliant piece of withholding — because it keeps us inside Tom's certainty while simultaneously making us feel its cost to Maggie.
The ruin has made Tom — and it has also made him capable of this kind of harm.
We've seen today how the ruin of one man sends fault lines through every relationship in the novel — through pride, through law, through the children who inherit both the debt and the fury.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — thank you.
In our next segment, we turn to Maggie herself — to what the novel asks of her, and what she asks of it.

segments.title: Eliot's Wit and Irony: How Narrative Creates Distance

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the programme where we read Eliot slowly enough to hear her thinking.
I'm joined today by three guests who bring very different instruments to the same score.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Eliot as a craftsperson reads a master cabinet-maker — always asking how it's done.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the measured judgement of a lifetime of Oxford scholarship and an unwavering belief that character, not circumstance, is the proper subject of fiction.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than most of us have read — he hears the prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Today's segment is on Eliot's wit and irony — specifically, how the narrative voice creates a kind of loving distance from its own characters.
Oliver, I want to start with you — because you've performed this novel, and you know in your bones where the comedy lives.
Thank you — and the comedy in this novel is something rather special, because it's never unkind and never cheap.
There's a chapter early on — Maggie running away to the gypsies — which is, I think, one of the funniest set-pieces in all of Victorian fiction.
Eliot gives us Maggie's imagination running riot — Apollyon, highwaymen, a blinking dwarf in yellow with a mouth from ear to ear.
And yet simultaneously she's narrating Maggie's social embarrassment with this perfectly calibrated deadpan.
Maggie hands her only sixpence to a pair of shabby men on the lane — her uncle Glegg's present, no less — in the hope that they'll think well of her generosity.
And then comes the line that floors me every time I read it aloud.
"It was clear that she was not likely to make a favourable impression on passengers."
That word 'passengers' — meaning passers-by — delivered with that perfect authorial neutrality.
It's devastating and tender at exactly the same moment.
What strikes me about that sentence is its structural position — it comes just after Maggie hears the men laughing at her.
Eliot doesn't give us Maggie's hurt directly — she gives us the narrator's cool assessment instead, and the hurt is in the gap between the two.
That's the ironic distance you're describing, Oliver — the narrator seeing more than the character, but never cruelty, always affection.
And what I love technically is that the comedy and the pathos are produced by the same device — the narrator's calm refusal to sentimentalise.
The passage actually tells us that Maggie has 'at once the timidity of an active imagination and the daring that comes from overmastering impulse.'
"She had at once the timidity of an active imagination and the daring that comes from overmastering impulse."
That's the whole of Maggie in one sentence — and it's comic in register, yet it's also the novel's thesis about her.
I think one must be careful not to reduce the irony here to a merely technical effect.
Eliot's distance from Maggie in this passage is the distance of moral wisdom — the narrator sees the child whole, as the child cannot see herself.
What is funny about Maggie giving away her last sixpence is not the act — the act is perfectly in keeping with her generous nature.
What is funny — and what is rather moving — is the gap between her expectation of gratitude and the man's rather dismissive 'Thank you, little miss.'
That is not irony as a literary device so much as irony as a condition of human experience.
Edmund, you're absolutely right — and it connects to something Eliot does with Bob Jakin later in the novel, which is a different register of comic entirely.
Bob is a natural-born salesman, and his technique with Mrs Glegg is a kind of masterclass in reverse psychology.
He holds up a piece of figured muslin and immediately tells her there's no point looking at it.
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
Then he flings it behind him on the turf — as if to save her eyes from it — before letting slip that the Princess Victoria herself might have worn it.
Eliot is writing pure comic theatre here — and the irony is that the narrator steps back entirely and just lets Bob perform.
The distance isn't between narrator and character this time — it's between Bob's magnificent shamelessness and Mrs Glegg's magnificent resistance.
That contrast is so well observed — because with Maggie, the narrator's distance is tender and slightly melancholy, even when it's funny.
With Bob, the narrator is simply delighted — she loves the performance as much as we do.
And there's a chapter — barely a paragraph, really — where Eliot deploys ironic distance with breathtaking economy.
The entire chapter opens with three words that function as both question and gentle mockery of the reader's anticipation.
"Had anything remarkable happened?"
That's the whole opening — and its comic force lies entirely in what the narrator knows and the reader suspects.
The ironic distance here is not from the character at all — it's from the very machinery of narrative expectation.
Three words — and yet they carry enormous weight, because by that point in the novel we know exactly what has happened.
What is interesting to me is how Eliot's irony changes register as the novel darkens.
By the time Philip Wakem writes his letter to Maggie, the narrator has almost entirely retired — and the irony, if one can call it that, is now Philip's own.
Philip sees clearly — the kind of clear sight that comes from suffering — and his letter is a document of almost painful lucidity.
He writes to Maggie — and here I think we must simply hear the sentence, because to paraphrase it is to diminish it —
"You have been to my affections what light, what colour is to my eyes, what music is to the inward ear, you have raised a dim unrest into a vivid consciousness."
That is not irony — that is its opposite — and yet it could not exist without all the ironic distance the novel has built before it.
Edmund has put his finger on something I've always felt when I read this novel aloud — the wit isn't separate from the pathos, it's the condition of it.
You can't have Philip's letter without the chapter of Bob Jakin selling muslin; you can't have that muslin scene without Maggie and her sixpence.
Eliot builds a world where the comedy and the tragedy are made of the same stuff — the gap between what we hope and what we receive.
That's a beautiful place to pause — the gap between hope and receipt as the engine of both comedy and tragedy in this novel.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the question of how Eliot shapes our sympathy — and whether there are characters she asks us to judge rather than love.

segments.title: Character Under Pressure: Bonds Tested and Moral Stakes Raised

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the Tulliver family's slow descent — financial, moral, emotional — and in this segment we're asking how characters reveal themselves under that pressure.
What does crisis strip away, and what does it lay bare?
I want to begin, though, with a figure who stands apart from the Tullivers entirely — the Reverend Walter Stelling.
Edmund, you've been given this portrait, and I suspect it pleases you enormously.
It pleases me immoderately, and I shall tell you why.
The portrait of Stelling is one of those passages in the novel where Eliot writes in the tradition of the great English comic moralists — Fielding, Johnson, even Gibbon.
She constructs a man who is entirely confident, entirely mediocre, and entirely unaware of the distinction.
Listen to how she describes his preaching — she tells us he had memorised passages of Massillon and Bourdaloue.

"Some passages of Massillon and Bourdaloue, which he knew by heart, were really very effective when rolled out in Mr Stelling's deepest tones; but as comparatively feeble appeals of his own were delivered in the same loud and impressive manner, they were often thought quite as striking by his hearers."
The hearers cannot tell the difference — and neither, crucially, can Stelling.
That is the moral joke at the heart of the passage, and it is devastating.
And the logic of debt — I adore the logic of debt in that passage.
She sets it out with the most perfect faux-syllogistic gravity, as though it were an argument in Euclid.
The furniture and the wine and the grand piano must be had — the only question is by what means.
"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting."
"Naturally" — that word is doing the most mischievous work in the sentence.
It's the narrator slipping inside Stelling's own reasoning and rendering it with complete, deadpan fidelity.
When I read that aloud in a recording, I always pause just a fraction before "naturally" — because the audience needs a beat to realise they're being shown something rather than told it.
What strikes me architecturally is the way Eliot holds Stelling at arm's length — but not contemptuous distance.
The free indirect discourse does something peculiar here — it mirrors Stelling's self-justifications so precisely that we feel the interiority, but the irony remains perfectly calibrated.
He has a true British determination — she even italicises the cliché, almost.
It's as though the narrator holds up the phrase in gloves, rather than bare hands.
And yet — this matters — Stelling is never simply mocked.
He is the instrument by which Tom and Maggie's education is botched — that has consequences the satire never lets us forget.
That is exactly the right word — instrument.
Stelling is comic, but the comedy is not merely decorative.
This is a man who will help shape — or rather, misshape — the character of Tom Tulliver at the most formative moment of his life.
That Tom emerges from Stelling's tutelage rigid, moralistic, and incapable of imaginative sympathy — that is, in part, Stelling's legacy.
And that rigidity in Tom leads us directly into the passages I want to turn to now.
The Tulliver family in crisis — the confrontation with Mrs Glegg, and then, most painfully, the father himself.
Edmund, you have what I think is one of the most quietly astonishing moments in the early part of the novel — Tom, at fifteen, holding himself together.
Quietly astonishing is precisely the phrase.
What Eliot gives us in this scene is something that cheap fiction would handle badly — the suppression of righteous anger in the service of duty.
Tom has just heard his aunt Glegg wound his mother; Maggie, all instinct and fire, is already on her feet.
And then the narrator steps back and says — in that characteristically level voice — something remarkable.

"It was a remarkable manifestation of self-command and practical judgment in a lad of fifteen, that when his aunt Glegg ceased, he began to speak in a quiet and respectful manner, though with a good deal of trembling in his voice; for his mother's words had cut him to the quick."
The trembling voice is what defeats me every time.
Tom controls his tongue, but not his body — and that physiological truth is what makes his self-command legible as genuine cost, not cold detachment.
The trembling voice — yes, and what a gift that is to a reader or an actor.
You cannot fake that detail; it could only come from someone who has observed genuine distress and genuine fortitude in the same person at the same moment.
And notice what Maggie does — she starts up, full impulse, and Tom simply says "Be quiet, Maggie" — pushing her aside.
That word "authoritatively" is doing something almost painful — because his authority at this moment is entirely earned.
He's not the bully he can sometimes be — he is, for this one scene, the best version of himself.
And that contrast with Maggie is structurally essential.
Eliot is showing us two different kinds of love — Maggie's as all motion, all exposure, and Tom's as containment, as the performance of composure under fire.
Neither is superior — and that is precisely what makes the novel's later tragedy so irreducible.
We have seen both siblings at their finest in the same moment of family danger — and we understand why they will still wound each other terribly.
Eleanor, I want to come to you now on a passage that feels to me like the emotional centre of this whole section of the novel.
The narrator's reflection on Maggie seeing her father's helplessness — what the novel calls one of those supreme moments.
This passage is, I think, one of the most beautiful single paragraphs Eliot ever wrote — and it is barely a paragraph.
It opens with something that should feel sentimental — "Poor child!" — but the exclamation is instantly redeemed by the philosophical precision that follows.
Let me read it — because it only works whole.
"Poor child! it was very early for her to know one of those supreme moments in life when all we have hoped or delighted in, all we can dread or endure, falls away from our regard as insignificant."
"Is lost, like a trivial memory, in that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
"Knits" — that verb is doing everything.
It suggests something made, something slow and domestic and bodily — not the romantic drama of love, but the woven fibre of it.
And "primitive" is equally precise — not primitive as primitive cultures, but as the original thing, the substrate beneath all other feeling.
When I record a passage like that, I find I have to stop before "in their times of helplessness or of anguish" — not for effect, but because the sentence genuinely earns a breath.
The prose rhythm slows of its own accord — those prepositional phrases accumulate like weights on a scale.
And "Poor child" at the opening — Edmund will tell me I'm wrong, but I hear something almost unbearable in that apostrophe.
The narrator is not at a cool distance here — the narrator is grieving alongside Maggie.
You are not wrong — and I find I cannot quite bring myself to say so.
What moves me here is the generalisation — "all we have hoped or delighted in."
Eliot moves from Maggie to all of us, with the quietest grammatical shift — from "her" to "we" — and in that shift, she makes Maggie's grief universal without diminishing it.
That is a moral imagination of the highest order — and I use the word moral advisedly.
And this love for the father — this primitive knitting — is precisely what makes the passages involving Mr Tulliver's own voice so devastating.
Edmund, you have two of them — and I think we should let them speak.
The first is from the terrible family reckoning after the bankruptcy — Mr Tulliver asking Tom to be still, seeking a moment of peace with his wife.
"Say no more, Tom, say no more; I've had enough for this day."
"Give me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
"This world's been too many for me" — a phrase of such Shakespearean plainness that I cannot read it without pause.
It is defeat rendered in the vernacular — not the language of tragedy but the language of exhaustion, of a man who has simply run out of world.
And the companion line — which Tulliver says directly to Maggie — is, if anything, more naked.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
Seven words — and an entire life's regret.
I have read that line aloud many times, and I still cannot find a way to protect myself from it.
"I shall never live twice o'er" — the dialect form "o'er" is doing something crucial here.
It is the voice of a man who has never had the luxury of fine language, speaking the deepest truth he knows in the only register he has.
And Eliot does not translate it or prettify it — she trusts it entirely.
That is, I think, an act of profound authorial respect.
The architecture of these two lines together is extraordinary — and I don't think it's accidental.
"We shall never be young again" is addressed to Bessy — it is about the marriage, the partnership, the shared diminishment of two people.
"I shall never live twice o'er" is addressed to Maggie — it is singular, private, the most intimate confession he is capable of.
Together they constitute a man saying farewell — to his marriage, to his ambitions, to his idea of himself — and he says it without a single word of self-pity.
That restraint — that is what Eliot understood about this kind of character that a lesser novelist would have sweetened into sentiment.
The word I keep returning to is dignity.
Tulliver is a broken man — legally, financially, spiritually.
But Eliot will not allow him to be merely pitiable.
His capacity to ask for a kiss, to seek reconciliation, to acknowledge defeat without evasion — these are moral acts, however small the theatre in which they occur.
That is what the novel insists upon — that goodness does not require a grand stage.
And perhaps that is exactly where we should rest — with goodness in the grain of the ordinary, under the weight of the unbearable.
Edmund Leigh, Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to what the novel does with time — memory, return, and the river that runs through all of it.

segments.title: Society's Script: Gender, Class, and Constraint in the Floss

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're exploring what the novel has to say about the invisible architecture of constraint — the forces of gender, class, and social expectation that shape every life in St Ogg's.

With me, as always, is Dr Eleanor Hartley — novelist, teacher of creative writing, and a critic who reads Eliot's sentences the way a watchmaker reads a movement: for the precision of every working part.
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us — retired Oxford don, moral reader of fiction, and a man who believes the novel's great subject is individual character under pressure, not social programme.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has voiced more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive, who hears in Eliot's prose the rhythms of a born performer.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with a moment that is almost comically small, yet somehow enormous.
Maggie Tulliver, aged about nine, pushes her cousin Lucy into the mud.
What is Eliot doing with that moment?
That passage stops me every time I read it — and I've read it many times.
What Eliot is doing there is structurally audacious.
She gives us the grandeur first — she actually uses the Greek, τι μέγεθος, the essential magnitude of tragedy.
And then the sentence pivots on that devastating 'but.'
The setup is almost Aristotelian in its solemnity — and then listen to where it lands.
"The utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud."
That compound adjective — pink-and-white — is doing extraordinary work.
It is the entire social script for femininity in a hyphenated phrase: delicate, ornamental, and perfectly clean.
And Maggie, with her small brown arm, destroys it — in a single sentence that manages to be tragic and absurdly funny at the same time.
That is the sentence that made me fall in love with this novel — and I mean that quite precisely.
Because as a performer, what I hear is a woman who has mastered comic timing to a degree that should embarrass the rest of us.
The elevation of the setup — the Greek, the Aristotle, the tragic machinery — all of it runs at full throttle.
And then: cow-trodden mud.
The rhythm of that landing — you can hear the splat.
But the genius — and Eleanor is absolutely right — is that the comedy doesn't dissolve the tragedy.
The tragedy is precisely that the passion is real and the mud is all there is.
I find myself in a curious position here — agreeing entirely with both of you, and wishing to add something that may seem unfashionable.
What strikes me is not the social commentary — which is present, and fine — but the moral weight.
Maggie's passions are at war, and the narrator names this with absolute clarity.
"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only."
That conditional — if tragedies were made by passion only — is a novelist's way of raising the stakes of the moral question.
What else is required for a life to constitute a tragedy?
Eliot is asking — with devastating gentleness — whether Maggie will ever be given the scale her nature demands.
Edmund, that's exactly where I want to go next — because this question of scale and constraint runs through the novel's treatment of fate itself.
There's a passage with Mr Tulliver that I think is one of the most quietly devastating in the entire book.
Tulliver has sworn he will never borrow from anyone connected to his enemy Wakem.
And yet — within a fortnight — Wakem's client is the only available lender.
The narrator's comment is almost insolently brief — and insolently brilliant.
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
Œdipus — a miller from the Floss.
That juxtaposition is audacious and compassionate at the same moment: Tulliver is not mocked, he is dignified, even as the irony shines through.
And the Œdipus comparison does something else a performer notices immediately — it's a structural signal.
Eliot is telling us that Tulliver is not simply unlucky — he is a man whose character and fate are woven together in exactly the way Greek tragedy requires.
His hatred of Wakem is not incidental; it is constitutive.
He cannot be Tulliver without that enmity — and so he cannot escape it.
This is the novel in its tragic mode — not satirical, not tender — but properly, weightily tragic.
What I find most moving — and I use that word with care — is the phrase 'inflicted on him rather than committed by him.'
That is not exculpation — Eliot is too honest for cheap exculpation.
It is, rather, a precise account of how character and circumstance collaborate in ruin.
Tulliver is not a victim — he is a man whose particular nature makes certain disasters almost inevitable.
Dr Johnson would have recognised him instantly.
This tension between the grand and the domestic, the tragic and the everyday — it's also present in the novel's treatment of home and memory.
Eleanor, you've brought another passage that I think speaks to this directly.
Yes — and this is Eliot in a completely different register: tender, pastoral, almost confessional.
It's a meditation on why we love the places we were born — and the argument she makes is quietly subversive.
She sets it up with the image of Tom returning home for the holidays — the light in the parlour, the warmth, the kisses.
And then she makes this claim about the nature of belonging.

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
'The labour of choice' — that phrase is the hinge of the whole argument.
Modernity asks us to choose everything — and Eliot is saying that the deepest attachments are the ones we never chose at all.
Which is, of course, also the trap that the novel will spring on Maggie with full force.
That observation strikes me as among the truest things in the novel.
Burke — and I invoke him quite deliberately — wrote that society is a contract between the dead, the living, and the yet unborn.
Eliot arrives at something very similar through the texture of a child's affection for a hearth-rug.
The elderberry bush is not a lesser object than the finest fuchsia — it is a different order of thing altogether.
It carries memory, and memory carries identity.
When the Tullivers lose the mill, they are not losing property — they are losing the conditions of their selfhood.
And Eliot dramatises that loss with one of the most unexpected scenes in the book — Mrs Tulliver and the linens.
Now, Mrs Tulliver is not, on the face of it, a figure of tragic dignity.
She is a worried, passive woman who talks about tablecloths at almost every crisis.
But when the sale of the household goods is imminent, something cracks open — and Eliot lets her speak.

"To think o' these cloths as I spun myself, and Job Haxey wove 'em, and brought the piece home on his back, as I remember standing at the door and seeing him come, before I ever thought o' marrying your father!"
You hear the whole arc of a life in that sentence.
The linen isn't just fabric — it is memory woven in, literally woven in, before the marriage, before the children, before the ruin.
And she goes on — she has chosen the pattern herself, she has marked it so that cutting would be the only way to erase her name.
It is, quietly, a portrait of female authorship — the only kind of authorship available to her.
Oliver, that's brilliant — and it connects directly to the way constraint works in this novel.
Mrs Tulliver's domain is the household — and she has made it her domain utterly, passionately, with real craft.
The marking so intricate it cannot be removed without cutting the cloth — that is a woman insisting on her own permanence within the only materials she was given.
And then the heartbreak: 'You'll never have one of 'em, my boy.'
Five words — and the whole meaning of the auction collapses into them.
Let's stay with constraint — but move now to the novel's fiercest confrontation with it.
Maggie and Tom — face to face, near the end, in one of the most scorching arguments in all of Victorian fiction.
Eleanor, this passage is yours — and it is, I think, among the hardest to read in the whole novel.
It really is — because Eliot allows Maggie to win the argument completely, and it changes nothing.
Maggie concedes her own wrongdoing first — 'I know I've been wrong, often, continually' — and that disarms the reader immediately.
But then she turns — and what she says is devastating in its precision.
"You have no pity; you have no sense of your own imperfection and your own sins.
It is a sin to be hard; it is not fitting for a mortal, for a Christian.
You are nothing but a Pharisee."
The word Pharisee lands like a verdict.
And the closing line — 'your shining virtues are mere darkness' — that is one of the great sentences in the novel.
I will not pretend this passage does not make me uncomfortable — it is intended to.
But I think the discomfort is moral, not political — and that is crucial.
Tom Tulliver is not a villain — he is a man of genuine virtue, limited imagination, and an almost complete absence of self-knowledge.
Eliot does not let Maggie off either — 'I know I've been wrong, often, continually' is not rhetorical.
But the line that is at the centre of the passage — that is the novel's moral centre — is this.
"You have not even a vision of feelings by the side of which your shining virtues are mere darkness."
Eliot is saying that virtue without sympathy is not virtue at all — it is simply the absence of a larger sight.
That is an argument I cannot dismiss — however much a part of me recognises Tom's position.
What stays with me as a performer is the rhetorical structure Eliot gives Maggie in that speech.
She builds in anaphora — 'you have always enjoyed... you have always been... you have no pity... you have no sense' — it is forensic, almost biblical in its repetition.
And then the final turn — the vision that Tom lacks — arrives not as anger but as something close to grief.
'You have not even a vision of feelings' — she is not condemning him; she is mourning the fact that he cannot see.
And that — that is what breaks you, when you read it aloud.
From childhood passion in the mud to a sister's indictment of her brother's righteousness — this novel never lets constraint go comfortably unexamined.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's ending — that flood, that reunion, that final silence — and asking what Eliot means by closing the story the way she does.

segments.title: Drowning and Transcendence: The Mill's Final Reckoning

utterances.text: We come now to the end — in every sense.
The closing chapters of The Mill on the Floss bring us to the flood, to death, to the strange hush that follows catastrophe.
But before we can understand what the ending means, we need to understand what has been lost — and what the novel has been building toward all along.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about the narrator's role in preparing us for this reckoning — the way childhood memory and landscape are woven into the novel's very foundations.
Yes — and I think this is where Eliot's architecture is most breathtaking.
From the very earliest chapters, she is constructing the emotional grammar that will make the ending devastating rather than merely dramatic.
The narrator makes an extraordinary claim about the English countryside — about what familiar landscapes actually do to us.

"These familiar flowers, these well-remembered bird-notes, this sky, with its fitful brightness, these furrowed and grassy fields, each with a sort of personality given to it by the capricious hedgerows."
And then she delivers the thesis: these things are, in her words, "the mother-tongue of our imagination."
That phrase — mother-tongue — is doing enormous work.
It tells us that the Floss, the mill, the fields — these are not backdrop; they are the language in which Maggie thinks and feels.
When the flood comes, it isn't an external catastrophe arriving from outside the story — it's the mother-tongue speaking its final word.
Eleanor has identified something essential, and I want to press on it from a slightly different angle.
One hears a good deal, nowadays, about Eliot's social commentary, her feminism, her critique of provincial life.
And while none of that is entirely wrong, it rather misses what I take to be the moral centre of the book.
The flood is not a verdict on society. It is the culmination of individual character tested to its absolute limit.
Maggie does not drown because the world has failed her — though it has.
She drowns in the act of recovering the one thing her entire life has strained toward — reunion with her brother.
That is a moral resolution of the most ancient and serious kind: sacrifice, recognition, and the final bond of love.
I agree with both of you, and I want to add something about how we arrive at the ending — which is to say, through Tom Tulliver.
Tom is not a sympathetic character in the way Maggie is — he is rigid, unforgiving, blinkered.
And yet Eliot gives him one of the most heartbreaking passages in the novel — a vision of his own diminishing hope.
"Two hours ago, as Tom was walking to St Ogg's, he saw the distant future before him as he might have seen a tempting stretch of smooth sandy beach beyond a belt of flinty shingles."
"But now his feet were on the sharp stones; the belt of shingles had widened, and the stretch of sand had dwindled into narrowness."
That image — the beach shrinking away just as you think you're nearly there — is one of the most truthful descriptions of disappointment I have ever read.
And it matters for the ending, because it shows us that Tom, too, has been ground down — that the novel's tragedy belongs to him as much as to Maggie.
And what's so remarkable is that Eliot never softens Tom to earn our sympathy — she shows us his inner life precisely as it is.
His cruelty to Maggie is real; his suffering is also real. The novel holds both without flinching.
Which makes Maggie's condition in those final chapters all the more annihilating.
She has been hollowed out by guilt and rejection until there is almost nothing left to wound.

"The idea of ever recovering happiness never glimmered in her mind for a moment; it seemed as if every sensitive fibre in her were too entirely preoccupied by pain ever to vibrate again to another influence."
That word — vibrate — is extraordinary. It's the language of music, of resonance.
Eliot is telling us that the instrument of Maggie's emotional life has been silenced — and yet the flood comes and strikes one last, overwhelming note.
That is beautifully put. Though I would add — it is not only Maggie's instrument that has been silenced.
Philip Wakem survives the flood, and in some ways his fate is the most quietly devastating in the novel.
He is left to a life of perfect, unanswerable solitude.
The narrator's account of him in the epilogue is, I think, among the most affecting things in the entire book.
"His great companionship was among the trees of the Red Deeps, where the buried joy seemed still to hover, like a revisiting spirit."
A revisiting spirit. He is haunted by the very happiness he was never quite permitted to possess.
That is George Eliot at her most morally serious: the punishment for nothing more than loving the wrong person, at the wrong time, in the wrong world.
"A revisiting spirit" — I've read that line aloud to audiences and you can hear the room go still.
There's something Eliot does at the very end that I think only she could bring off — she earns the tragedy so completely that the reader feels it as grief, not as literary effect.
The flood is monstrous and also, somehow, right — because the Floss has been present on every page, waiting.
Eleanor's phrase — the mother-tongue — captures it exactly. The river is the first word and the last.
The river as the first word and the last — I can't imagine a better note on which to end.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you for a conversation that has done genuine justice to one of the great novels in the English language.
The Mill on the Floss asks more of its readers than almost any other Victorian novel — more patience with ordinary life, more willingness to sit with suffering that has no clean resolution.
And in return it gives back everything — a world so fully imagined that losing it feels like a bereavement.
Thank you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c14:p100.text:
But when this small apparatus of shallow quickness was fetched away in the gig
by Luke, and the study was once more quite lonely for Tom, he missed her
grievously. He had really been brighter, and had got through his lessons
better, since she had been there; and she had asked Mr Stelling so many
questions about the Roman Empire, and whether there really ever was a man who
said, in Latin, “I would not buy it for a farthing or a rotten
nut,” or whether that had only been turned into Latin, that Tom had
actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been
people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning
it through the medium of the Eton Grammar. This luminous idea was a great
addition to his historical acquirements during this half-year, which were
otherwise confined to an epitomised history of the Jews.
c14:p100.summary: Tom grieves Maggie's departure and credits her insightful questions about the Roman Empire with expanding his historical understanding beyond his textbooks.
c14:p100.best_quote: he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c14:p11.text:
Yet, strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl
than he had ever been in his life before. He had a large share of pride, which
had hitherto found itself very comfortable in the world, despising Old Goggles,
and reposing in the sense of unquestioned rights; but now this same pride met
with nothing but bruises and crushings. Tom was too clear-sighted not to be
aware that Mr Stelling’s standard of things was quite different, was
certainly something higher in the eyes of the world than that of the people he
had been living amongst, and that, brought in contact with it, he, Tom
Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid; he was by no means indifferent to this,
and his pride got into an uneasy condition which quite nullified his boyish
self-satisfaction, and gave him something of the girl’s susceptibility.
He was of a very firm, not to say obstinate, disposition, but there was no
brute-like rebellion and recklessness in his nature; the human sensibilities
predominated, and if it had occurred to him that he could enable himself to
show some quickness at his lessons, and so acquire Mr Stelling’s
approbation, by standing on one leg for an inconvenient length of time, or
rapping his head moderately against the wall, or any voluntary action of that
sort, he would certainly have tried it. But no; Tom had never heard that these
measures would brighten the understanding, or strengthen the verbal memory; and
he was not given to hypothesis and experiment. It did occur to him that he
could perhaps get some help by praying for it; but as the prayers he said every
evening were forms learned by heart, he rather shrank from the novelty and
irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic of petition for
which he was not aware of any precedent. But one day, when he had broken down,
for the fifth time, in the supines of the third conjugation, and Mr Stelling,
convinced that this must be carelessness, since it transcended the bounds of
possible stupidity, had lectured him very seriously, pointing out that if he
failed to seize the present golden opportunity of learning supines, he would
have to regret it when he became a man,—Tom, more miserable than usual,
determined to try his sole resource; and that evening, after his usual form of
prayer for his parents and “little sister” (he had begun to pray
for Maggie when she was a baby), and that he might be able always to keep
God’s commandments, he added, in the same low whisper, “and please
to make me always remember my Latin.” He paused a little to consider how
he should pray about Euclid—whether he should ask to see what it meant,
or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to
the case. But at last he added: “And make Mr Stelling say I
sha’n’t do Euclid any more. Amen.”
c14:p11.summary: Humiliated by repeated failures, Tom resorts to prayer, adding petitions for Latin and Euclid to his nightly prayers, showing his desperation and underlying sensitivity.
c14:p11.best_quote: and please to make me always remember my Latin

c51:p29.text:
But to minds strongly marked by the positive and negative qualities that create
severity,—strength of will, conscious rectitude of purpose, narrowness of
imagination and intellect, great power of self-control, and a disposition to
exert control over others,—prejudices come as the natural food of
tendencies which can get no sustenance out of that complex, fragmentary,
doubt-provoking knowledge which we call truth. Let a prejudice be bequeathed,
carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the
eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is
something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of
spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of
conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton. Every prejudice that will
answer these purposes is self-evident. Our good, upright Tom Tulliver’s
mind was of this class; his inward criticism of his father’s faults did
not prevent him from adopting his father’s prejudice; it was a prejudice
against a man of lax principle and lax life, and it was a meeting-point for all
the disappointed feelings of family and personal pride. Other feelings added
their force to produce Tom’s bitter repugnance to Philip, and to
Maggie’s union with him; and notwithstanding Lucy’s power over her
strong-willed cousin, she got nothing but a cold refusal ever to sanction such
a marriage; “but of course Maggie could do as she liked,—she had
declared her determination to be independent. For Tom’s part, he held
himself bound by his duty to his father’s memory, and by every manly
feeling, never to consent to any relation with the Wakems.”
c51:p29.summary: The narrator characterizes Tom's mind as rigid and wedded to inherited prejudice; his narrow imagination and strong will make him incapable of questioning paternal grievances or considering Maggie's happiness with Philip.
c51:p29.best_quote: Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right

c37:p70.text:
“Don’t talk high-flown nonsense to me, sir! Do you mean to pretend
that you didn’t know it would be injurious to her to meet you here week
after week? Do you pretend you had any right to make professions of love to
her, even if you had been a fit husband for her, when neither her father nor
your father would ever consent to a marriage between you? And
 you ,— you  to try and worm yourself into the affections of a
handsome girl who is not eighteen, and has been shut out from the world by her
father’s misfortunes! That’s your crooked notion of honour, is it?
I call it base treachery; I call it taking advantage of circumstances to win
what’s too good for you,—what you’d never get by fair
means.”

c37:p53.text:
“Do what  I  require,” said Tom. “I can’t trust
you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you. Put your hand on this Bible, and
say, ‘I renounce all private speech and intercourse with Philip Wakem
from this time forth.’ Else you will bring shame on us all, and grief on
my father; and what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything
else for the sake of paying my father’s debts, if you are to bring
madness and vexation on him, just when he might be easy and hold up his head
once more?”

c32:p37.text:
At last Maggie’s eyes glanced down on the books that lay on the
window-shelf, and she half forsook her reverie to turn over listlessly the
leaves of the “Portrait Gallery,” but she soon pushed this aside to
examine the little row of books tied together with string. “Beauties of
the Spectator,” “Rasselas,” “Economy of Human
Life,” “Gregory’s Letters,”—she knew the sort of
matter that was inside all these; the “Christian Year,”—that
seemed to be a hymnbook, and she laid it down again; but  Thomas à
Kempis? —the name had come across her in her reading, and she felt the
satisfaction, which every one knows, of getting some ideas to attach to a name
that strays solitary in the memory. She took up the little, old, clumsy book
with some curiosity; it had the corners turned down in many places, and some
hand, now forever quiet, had made at certain passages strong pen-and-ink marks,
long since browned by time. Maggie turned from leaf to leaf, and read where the
quiet hand pointed: “Know that the love of thyself doth hurt thee more
than anything in the world.... If thou seekest this or that, and wouldst be
here or there to enjoy thy own will and pleasure, thou shalt never be quiet nor
free from care; for in everything somewhat will be wanting, and in every place
there will be some that will cross thee.... Both above and below, which way
soever thou dost turn thee, everywhere thou shalt find the Cross; and
everywhere of necessity thou must have patience, if thou wilt have inward
peace, and enjoy an everlasting crown.... If thou desirest to mount unto this
height, thou must set out courageously, and lay the axe to the root, that thou
mayest pluck up and destroy that hidden inordinate inclination to thyself, and
unto all private and earthly good. On this sin, that a man inordinately loveth
himself, almost all dependeth, whatsoever is thoroughly to be overcome; which
evil being once overcome and subdued, there will presently ensue great peace
and tranquillity.... It is but little thou sufferest in comparison of them that
have suffered so much, were so strongly tempted, so grievously afflicted, so
many ways tried and exercised. Thou oughtest therefore to call to mind the more
heavy sufferings of others, that thou mayest the easier bear thy little
adversities. And if they seem not little unto thee, beware lest thy impatience
be the cause thereof.... Blessed are those ears that receive the whispers of
the divine voice, and listen not to the whisperings of the world. Blessed are
those ears which hearken not unto the voice which soundeth outwardly, but unto
the Truth, which teacheth inwardly.”
c32:p37.summary: Maggie picks up Thomas à Kempis' Imitation of Christ and reads passages of spiritual wisdom about renouncing self-love and pride, marked long ago by an unknown previous reader.
c32:p37.best_quote: Know that the love of thyself doth hurt thee more than anything in the world.... If thou seekest this or that, and wouldst be here or there to enjoy thy own will and pleasure, thou shalt never be quiet nor free from care

c13:p5.text:

leave you to judge what effect was produced on her by the reception of a short
letter from Mr Tulliver that very evening, after Mrs Pullet’s
departure, informing her that she needn’t trouble her mind about her five
hundred pounds, for it should be paid back to her in the course of the next
month at farthest, together with the interest due thereon until the time of
payment. And furthermore, that Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to
Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he
desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
